name: Job
sourceNote: Translated from the Hebrew of the Westminster Leningrad Codex, checked against the Septuagint and against the Aramaic Targum of Job found at Qumran (11QtgJob, which preserves parts of chapters 17–42, and a small fragment from Cave 4, 4QtgJob). Job is mostly poetry, printed here line by line; its Hebrew contains more rare words and words found only once in the Bible (hapax legomena) than any other book, and many lines are uncertain; the footnotes say so. The Old Greek (Septuagint) Job was about one-sixth shorter than the Hebrew; the missing lines were later filled in from the Greek version of Theodotion and are not marked in Brenton’s English, so footnotes describe these gaps in general terms. The Septuagint also adds a longer speech by Job’s wife (2:9) and a longer ending (42:17). Every Septuagint reading cited was checked against Brenton’s public-domain English translation (quoted in modernized wording). Readings of 11QtgJob are stated in general terms (“is reported to read”) until they can be checked against the critical edition. Identifications of animals, plants, and precious stones are often uncertain and are footnoted. Verse numbers follow the standard English Bible; where the Hebrew numbering differs (41:1–34), a footnote says so. The Hebrew name of God, YHWH, is written “Yahweh”; Shaddai is kept as a name (see the note at 5:17).

verses.text: There was a man in the land of Uz{a} whose name was Job.{b} And that man was blameless and upright, one who feared God and turned aside from evil.
There were born to him seven sons and three daughters.

His livestock was seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys, and a very great body of servants; so that this man was greater than all the sons of the east.{c}
It was the custom of his sons to go and make a feast, each at his own house on his own day; and they would send and call their three sisters to eat and drink along with them.

And when the days of the feasting had gone round, Job would send and sanctify them, and he would rise early in the morning and offer burnt offerings according to the number of them all. For Job said, “It may be that my sons have sinned and have blessed{d} God in their hearts.” Thus Job did all the days.
Now there was a day when the sons of God{e} came to present themselves before Yahweh, and the Adversary{f} also came among them.
Yahweh said to the Adversary, “From where do you come?” Then the Adversary answered Yahweh and said, “From roaming through the earth and from walking to and fro in it.”
And Yahweh said to the Adversary, “Have you set your heart upon my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a man blameless and upright, one who fears God and turns aside from evil?”
Then the Adversary answered Yahweh and said, “Is it for nothing that Job fears God?
Have you not hedged him about, and his house, and all that he has, on every side? The work of his hands you have blessed, and his livestock has burst out in the land.
But stretch out your hand now and touch all that he has, and surely he will bless{g} you to your face.”
And Yahweh said to the Adversary, “Look, all that he has is in your hand; only upon himself do not put forth your hand.” So the Adversary went out from the presence of Yahweh.
Now there was a day when his sons and his daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their brother the firstborn,
and a messenger came to Job and said, “The oxen were plowing and the donkeys grazing beside them,
and Sabeans{h} fell upon them and took them, and the servants they struck with the edge of the sword; and I alone, only I, have escaped to tell you.”
While he was yet speaking, another came and said, “The fire of God{i} fell from the heavens and burned up the sheep and the servants and consumed them; and I alone, only I, have escaped to tell you.”

While he was yet speaking, another came and said, “Chaldeans formed three companies and made a raid upon the camels and took them, and the servants they struck with the edge of the sword; and I alone, only I, have escaped to tell you.”
While he was yet speaking, another came and said, “Your sons and your daughters were eating and drinking wine in the house of their brother the firstborn,
and look, a great wind came from across the wilderness and struck the four corners of the house, and it fell upon the young people, and they are dead; and I alone, only I, have escaped to tell you.”
Then Job arose and tore his robe and shaved his head, and he fell to the ground and bowed down.
Through all of this Job sinned not, nor did he lay anything unseemly{k} to God’s charge.

notes.text: The location of Uz is uncertain; it was probably east or southeast of Israel, in or near Edom (compare Lamentations 4:21). The Septuagint’s ending (see the note at 42:17) places it “on the borders of Idumea and Arabia” (Brenton).
The meaning of the name Job (Hebrew ʾIyyov) is uncertain; proposals include “Where is the father?” and “one who is hostile.”
That is, the peoples east of Israel, in the Syrian and Arabian desert.
Hebrew “blessed,” used here and in 1:11, 2:5, and 2:9 as a euphemism for “cursed”; scribes apparently avoided writing “curse God.”
Hebrew bene ha-ʾelohim, heavenly beings of the divine court; so also 2:1 and 38:7. The Septuagint reads “the angels of God” (Brenton).

Hebrew ha-satan, “the satan,” that is, “the adversary” or “the accuser.” With the article it is a title or role in the heavenly court, not yet a personal name; so throughout chapters 1–2. The Septuagint reads “the devil” (Brenton).
Hebrew “bless”; see the note at 1:5.
The Sabeans were probably raiders from Sheba in southern Arabia; the Septuagint reads “the spoilers” (Brenton).
Or “a terrible fire,” probably lightning.
That is, to the earth, pictured as the mother of all (compare Psalm 139:15), or to the grave.
Or “nor did he charge God with wrongdoing”; Hebrew tiflah, “unseemliness.”

verses.text: Again there was a day when the sons of God came to present themselves before Yahweh, and the Adversary also came among them to present himself before Yahweh.
And Yahweh said to the Adversary, “From where do you come?” Then the Adversary answered Yahweh and said, “From roaming through the earth and from walking to and fro in it.”

Yahweh said to the Adversary, “Have you set your heart upon my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth, a man blameless and upright, one who fears God and turns aside from evil? And he still holds fast his integrity, although you incited me against him to swallow him up for no cause.”
Then the Adversary answered Yahweh and said, “Skin for skin!{a} All that a man has he will give for his life.
But stretch out your hand now and touch his bone and his flesh, and surely he will bless{b} you to your face.”
And Yahweh said to the Adversary, “Look, he is in your hand; only spare his life.”
So the Adversary went out from the presence of Yahweh and struck Job with grievous sores{c} from the sole of his foot to his crown.
And he took for himself a potsherd to scrape himself with, while he sat in the midst of the ashes.{d}
Then his wife said to him, “Do you still hold fast your integrity? Bless{e} God, and die.”{f}
But he said to her, “You speak as one of the foolish women speaks. Shall we indeed receive the good from God, and the evil we shall not receive?” In all this Job did not sin with his lips.

Now when Job’s three friends heard of all this evil that had come upon him, they came each from his own place: Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite.{g} And they made an appointment together to come to show him sympathy and to comfort him.
And when they lifted up their eyes from afar and did not recognize him, they lifted up their voices and wept; and they tore each his robe and sprinkled dust upon their heads toward the heavens.
And they sat with him upon the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spoke a word to him, for they saw that his pain was very great.

notes.text: Probably a proverb from barter: a man will give up one hide to save another, or any possession to save his own skin. The exact sense is uncertain.
Hebrew “bless”; see the note at 1:5.
Hebrew shekhin raʿ; perhaps boils or a skin disease; the exact illness cannot be identified.
The Septuagint reads “and sat upon a dung-heap outside the city” (Brenton, modernized).
Hebrew “bless”; see the note at 1:5.

The Septuagint has a much longer speech here, in which Job’s wife laments their lost children and her own wandering “from place to place and house to house,” ending “but say some word against the Lord, and die” (Brenton, modernized).

Eliphaz perhaps means “God is fine gold” (uncertain); Teman was a region of Edom. Bildad perhaps means “Bel has loved” or “son of Hadad” (uncertain); Shuah was a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Zophar perhaps means “sparrow” or “twitterer” (uncertain); Naamah’s location is unknown. The Septuagint calls them “Eliphaz the king of the Temanites, Bildad sovereign of the Shuhites, Zophar king of the Minaeans” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text: After this Job opened his mouth and cursed his day.
And Job answered and said:

“Perish the day wherein I was to be born,
and the night which said, ‘A male has been conceived!’

That day—let it be darkness!
Let not God above seek after it,
nor light shine upon it.

Look, let that night be barren;
let no shout of joy come into it.

Let those who curse the day lay a curse on it,
those who are skilled to rouse up Leviathan.{c}

because it did not shut the doors of my mother’s womb,
nor hide trouble from my eyes.

“Why did I not die from the womb,
come out from the belly and breathe my last?

Why did knees receive me?
And why breasts, that I should suck?

For by now I would be lying down at rest;
I would be asleep; it would be repose for me,

with kings and counselors of the earth,
who rebuilt ruins{d} for themselves,

or with princes who had gold,
who filled their houses with silver.

Or like a hidden stillbirth I would not be,
like infants who never saw light.

There the wicked cease from troubling,
and there the weary in strength are at rest.

Together the prisoners are at ease;
they hear not the voice of the taskmaster.

The small and the great are there,
and the slave is free from his master.

“Why is light given to him who is in misery,
and life to the bitter of soul,

who long for death, but it comes not,
and dig for it more than for hidden treasures,

who rejoice to exultation
and are glad when they find a grave?

Why is light given to a man whose way is hidden,
whom God has hedged in?

For my sighing comes before my bread,{e}
and my groanings are poured out like water.

For the thing I feared has come upon me,
and what I dreaded comes to me.

I am not at ease, nor am I quiet,
nor have I rest; but turmoil comes.”

notes.text: Hebrew tsalmawet, traditionally “shadow of death”; many scholars read it as tsalmut, “deep darkness.” So throughout Job.
Hebrew kimrire yom, a rare word; perhaps eclipses or the darkenings of the day, or “bitterness of the day” (uncertain).

Leviathan is a sea monster of ancient Near Eastern myth, a symbol of chaos (compare 41:1; Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1). Some scholars, by a slight change, read “those who curse the sea (yam).” The Septuagint reads “he that is ready to attack the great sea monster” (Brenton, modernized: “the great whale”).
Or “built tombs” (perhaps pyramids); the Hebrew is uncertain. The Septuagint reads “who gloried in their swords” (Brenton).
Or “in place of my bread,” or “at the sight of my food.”

verses.text: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:

“If one ventures a word to you, will you be wearied?
Yet who can hold back from speaking?

Look, you have instructed many,
and slack hands you have made strong.

The one who was stumbling your words have lifted up,
and knees that bowed you have made firm.

But now it has come to you, and you are wearied;
it touches you, and you are dismayed.

Is not your fear of God your confidence,
and your hope the blamelessness of your ways?

“Recall, I beg you: what guiltless man has perished?
And where have upright men been cut off?

Even as I have observed: plowers of wickedness,
and sowers of mischief—the same they harvest.

By the breath of God they perish,
and by the blast of his anger they are consumed.

The roar of the lion and the voice of the fierce lion,
and the teeth of the young lions—they are broken.{a}

The old lion perishes for want of prey,
and the cubs of the lioness are scattered.

“Now to me a word came stealing,
and my ear received a whisper of it.

Amid disquieting thoughts from visions of the night,
when deep sleep falls upon men,

dread came upon me, and trembling,
and the multitude of my bones it made to shake.

Then a spirit{b} glided past my face;
the hair of my flesh stood on end.

‘Shall mortal man be just in the sight of God?{c}
Or shall a man be clean in the sight of the one who made him?

Look, in his servants he puts no trust,
and to his angels he charges error.{d}

How much more those who dwell in houses of clay,
whose foundation is in the dust,
who are crushed sooner than the moth!

Between morning and evening they are beaten to pieces;
without anyone heeding, they perish forever.

Is not their tent-cord{e} pulled up within them?
They die, and not in wisdom.’

notes.text: Five different Hebrew words for lion appear in 4:10–11 (ʾaryeh, shaḥal, kefir, layish, and lavi); their exact distinctions are uncertain.
Or “a wind” or “a breath.”
Hebrew Eloah, a poetic singular of Elohim; it occurs about forty times in Job and is translated “God.” Or “more righteous than God … more pure than his Maker.”
Hebrew toholah, found only here (a hapax legomenon); the meaning is uncertain, perhaps “error” or “folly.”
Or “their excellence”; the Hebrew yeter can mean a tent-cord or what is left over.

verses.text:
“Cry out, then! Is there one to answer you?
To which among the holy ones{a} would you turn?

Surely resentment slays the foolish,
and envy puts the gullible to death.

With my own eyes I saw a fool striking root,
and at once I pronounced his homestead cursed.

His sons are far from safety;
they are crushed in the gate, and there is none to deliver.

For mischief springs not up out of the dust,
nor from the soil does misery sprout;

but man is born to trouble,
as the sons of Resheph{d} fly upward.

“But I—I would inquire of God,
and before God I would lay my case,

who does great things beyond searching out,
wonders without number;

who gives rain upon the face of the earth
and sends waters upon the face of the fields;

to set the lowly up on high,
and mourners are raised to safety.

He frustrates the plans of the crafty,
so that their hands achieve nothing lasting.{e}

He takes the wise in their own craftiness,{f}
and the counsel of the twisted is swept headlong.

By day they meet with darkness,
and at noon they grope as in the night.

But he saves from the sword of their mouth,
and from the hand of the strong, the needy.

So the poor has hope,
and injustice shuts her mouth.

“Look, happy is the man whom God reproves;
so do not reject the discipline of Shaddai.{g}

For he wounds, but he binds up;
he smites, and his hands heal.

In six troubles he will deliver you,
and in seven no evil shall touch you.

In famine he redeems you from death,
and in war from the hand of the sword.

From the scourge of the tongue you shall be hidden,
and you shall not fear destruction when it comes.

At destruction and at hunger you shall laugh,
and of the beasts of the earth you shall not be afraid.

For with the stones of the field you shall be in covenant,
and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.

You shall know your tent to be in peace;
you shall visit your pasture-place and find nothing gone astray.

You shall know your seed to be numerous,
your offspring as the herbage of the ground.

You shall come to the grave in ripe old age,{h}
as a sheaf goes up in its season.

Look, this we have searched out; so it is.
Hear it, and know it for yourself.”

notes.text: That is, heavenly beings.
The Hebrew of this line is obscure.
So several ancient versions (Aquila, Symmachus, the Syriac, and the Vulgate, reading tsemeʾim); the Hebrew word tsammim is uncertain, often taken as “a snare.”

Resheph was a Canaanite god of plague and fire; “the sons of Resheph” may be sparks or birds of prey. Or “as sparks fly upward.” The Septuagint reads “the vulture’s young seek the high places” (Brenton).
Hebrew tushiyyah, a word of uncertain meaning found mostly in Job and Proverbs: “success,” “sound wisdom,” or “lasting result.”
Quoted in 1 Corinthians 3:19.
Hebrew Shaddai, a divine name traditionally rendered “the Almighty”; its meaning is uncertain (see the note at Genesis 17:1). It occurs 31 times in Job and is kept as a name throughout.
Hebrew kelaḥ, found only here and in 30:2; the meaning “full vigor” or “ripe age” is a guess from context.

verses.text: Then Job answered and said:

“O that my vexation were but weighed,
and my calamity laid with it in the balances!

For now it would be heavier than the sand of the seas;
therefore my words have been rash.{a}

Does the wild donkey bray over the grass,
or does the ox low over its fodder?

Can what is tasteless be eaten without salt,
or is there any flavor in the slime of the purslane?{b}

My soul refuses to touch them;
they are like sickness in my food.{c}

“O that my request might come,
and that God would grant my hope,

that it would please God to crush me,
that he would let loose his hand and cut me off!

Then this would still be my comfort,
and I would leap for joy{d} in pain that does not spare,
that I have not hidden the words of the Holy One.

What is my strength, that I should wait?
And what is my end, that I should prolong my life?

Is my strength the strength of stones,
or is my flesh bronze?

Is not my help within me gone,
and sound wisdom{e} driven away from me?

“To one who is fainting, kindness is owed from his friend,
even if he forsakes the fear of Shaddai.{f}

My brothers have dealt deceitfully like a wadi,
like the channels of wadis that pass away,

which are dark with ice,
where the snow hides itself;

at the time they are scorched, they vanish;
when it is hot, they are extinguished from their place.

Caravans swerve from off their way;
up into the empty waste they go, and perish.

The caravans out of Tema have looked for them;
on them the companies of Sheba set their hope.

They are ashamed because they trusted;
they come there and are confounded.

For now you have become nothing;{g}
you see a terror, and are afraid.

Did I say, ‘Give to me,’
or, ‘From your wealth offer a bribe for me,’

or, ‘Deliver me from the hand of the foe,’
and, ‘From the hand of the ruthless ransom me’?

“Teach me, and I will be silent;
and make me understand how I have erred.

How forceful are upright words!
But what does your reproving reprove?

Do you intend to reprove words,
while the speeches of one in despair are for the wind?

Over an orphan you would even throw the lot,
and over your companion you would haggle.

But now, be pleased to look at me;
for to your faces I will surely not lie.

Turn back, I pray; let there be no injustice;
turn back again; my righteousness is still in it.

Is there injustice on my tongue?
Can my palate not discern calamities?

notes.text: Hebrew laʿu, a rare verb; perhaps “wild” or “stammering.”
Hebrew ḥallamut, found only here; perhaps the juice of a mallow or purslane plant, or the white of an egg (so the Targum and many interpreters). The identification is uncertain.
The Hebrew of this line is uncertain.
Hebrew saledah, found only here; the meaning “leap” or “exult” is uncertain (perhaps “recoil”).
Hebrew tushiyyah; see the note at 5:12.
The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.

The Hebrew is difficult: the written text has lo, “not,” and the scribal reading is lo, “to it.” Many read “For now you have become like it,” that is, like the dried-up wadi. The Septuagint reads “But you also have come to me without pity” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text:
“Has not man a time of hard service upon earth,
and are not his days like the days of a hired laborer?

As a servant pants for shade,
as a hireling looks for the pay of his work,

so I have been allotted months of emptiness,
and nights of trouble have been appointed to me.

My flesh is clothed with worms and clods of dust;
my skin hardens and then runs again.

Swifter are my days than the shuttle of a weaver,
and they are spent with no hope remaining.{b}

“Remember that my life is a breath;
my eye will not again see good.

The eye of him who sees me will behold me no more;
your eyes will be upon me, but I shall not be.

As a cloud fades and goes away,
so he who goes down to Sheol{c} does not come up.

He shall not return again to his house,
nor shall his place know him anymore.

Am I Sea, or am I Dragon,{d}
that over me you post a watch?

When I say, ‘My bed will comfort me,
my couch will ease my complaint,’

then you terrify me with dreams
and affright me with visions,

so that my soul would choose strangling,
death rather than these bones of mine.

I loathe it; I would not live forever.
Leave me alone, for my days are a breath.

“What is man, that you should make so much of him,
and that you should set your heart upon him,

and visit him every morning,
and test him every moment?

How long will you not look away from me,
nor let me alone till I swallow my spittle?

If I have sinned, what do I do to you,
O watcher of mankind?
Why have you set me as your target,
so that I am a burden to myself?{e}

And why do you not pardon my transgression
and take away my iniquity?
For now I shall lie down in the dust;
and you will seek me diligently, but I shall not be.”

notes.text: Hebrew middad, uncertain; perhaps “the evening stretches out.”
Hebrew tiqwah, “hope,” also means “thread” or “cord” (Joshua 2:18); a wordplay with the weaver’s shuttle.
Sheol is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead.
Hebrew tannin, a sea dragon of ancient myth; compare 3:8.
So the standard Hebrew text; an ancient scribal tradition (one of the “corrections of the scribes”) and the Septuagint read “a burden to you” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:

“How long will you speak these things,
and the words of your mouth be a mighty wind?

Does God pervert justice,
or does Shaddai pervert what is right?

If your sons have sinned against him,
he has sent them away into the hand of their transgression.

If you yourself will seek God earnestly
and make supplication to Shaddai,

And though your beginning was small,
your latter end would grow very great.

“For ask, I pray, of the former generation,
and set yourself to what their fathers searched out.

For we are of yesterday and know nothing,
because our days upon earth are a shadow.

Shall not they instruct you, speak to you,
and from out of their heart bring forth words?

Does the papyrus{a} rise up without a swamp?
Does the rush grow tall without water?

While it is yet in its green shoot, not cut down,
before any other grass it withers.

Such are the paths of all who forget God;
and the hope of the godless shall perish.

His confidence is cut off,{b}
and his trust is a spider’s house.{c}

He leans upon his house, but it does not stand;
he grasps hold of it, but it does not endure.

He is a well-watered plant before the sun,
and over his garden his shoots go forth.

Over a heap of stones his roots are entwined;
he gazes upon a house of stones.{d}

If he is swallowed up from his place,
then it will deny him: ‘I never saw you.’

Look, this is the joy of his way,{e}
and from the dust others will spring up.

“See, God spurns not the man of integrity,
nor does he grasp the hand of doers of evil.

Yet once more he will fill your mouth with laughing,
and your lips with a joyful shout.

Those who hate you shall be clothed with shame,
and the tent of the wicked shall be no more.”

notes.text: Hebrew gomeʾ, the papyrus plant of the Nile marshes.
Hebrew yaqot, found only here; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps “is a gossamer thread” or “is cut off.”
That is, a spider’s web.
Or “he lives among stones”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
That is, ironically, this is how his “joy” ends.

verses.text: Then Job answered and said:

“Truly I know that it is so;
but how can a man be in the right with God?

Should one desire to go to law with him,
not once in a thousand times could he reply to him.

He is wise in heart and mighty in strength;
who has hardened himself against him and been unharmed?

He who removes mountains, and they know it not,
when he overturns them in his anger;

who shakes the earth out of its place,
and its pillars tremble;

who speaks to the sun, and it does not rise,
and sets a seal upon the stars;

who alone stretches out the heavens
and treads upon the heights{a} of the sea;

who made the Bear, Orion, and the Pleiades,{b}
and the chambers of the south;

who does great things beyond searching out,
and wonders without number.

He goes by beside me, and I behold him not;
he sweeps on, and I have no perception of him.

He seizes, and who can make him give it back?
Who shall say to him, ‘What is this you do?’

“God turns not back his wrath;
under him the allies of Rahab{c} lay bowed.

How much less shall I answer him,
choosing my words with him?

Though I were in the right, I could not answer;
to my judge I would have to plead for mercy.

Should I call and he answer me,
I could not trust that my voice had his ear.

For he crushes me with a tempest
and multiplies my wounds without cause.

He does not allow me to draw my breath again,
but sates me with bitter things.

If it is a matter of strength, look, he is mighty!
And if of justice, who will summon me?{d}

Were I in the right, my mouth itself would declare me guilty;
were I without blame, it would show me crooked.

I am blameless; I do not regard myself;
I loathe my life.

It is all one; therefore I say,
‘The blameless and the wicked he brings to an end.’

When a scourge kills suddenly,
he mocks at the despair of the innocent.

“My days are swifter than a runner;
they flee away; they see no good.

They have slipped by like boats of reed,{e}
like an eagle that swoops upon its food.

If I say, ‘I will forget my complaint,
I will put off my sad face and be cheerful,’

I shrink in fear from all my pains;
I know you will not count me guiltless.

I shall be condemned;
why then do I labor in vain?

If I wash myself with snow
and cleanse my hands with lye,{f}

even then into the ditch you would dip me,
and my garments would find me loathsome.

For he is not a man, as I am, that I might answer him,
that we should come together in judgment.

Between us no umpire{g} stands,
to rest his hand upon the two of us.

Let him take his rod away from me,
and let not dread of him terrify me.

Then I would speak and not fear him;
for I am not so in myself.

notes.text: Hebrew “the backs” (bamote), which may mean the waves or the back of the sea monster; compare 3:8.

The identification of these constellations (Hebrew ʿash, kesil, and kimah) is uncertain; compare 38:31–32 and Amos 5:8. The Septuagint reads “the Pleiades, and Hesperus, and Arcturus” (Brenton, modernized).

Rahab is a mythic sea monster representing chaos (compare 26:12; Psalm 89:10; Isaiah 51:9), not the woman of Jericho; the names are spelled differently in Hebrew. The Septuagint reads “the sea monsters under heaven” (Brenton, modernized: “the whales”).
The Hebrew may be quoting God’s reply; many read “who can summon him?” The Septuagint reads “who then shall resist his judgment?” (Brenton). The line is uncertain.
Light boats made of papyrus reeds (Isaiah 18:2).
Hebrew bor, a cleansing agent made from plant ash.
Or “umpire” or “mediator”; Hebrew mokiaḥ. Some Hebrew manuscripts read “O that there were an arbiter between us”; compare the Septuagint, “Would that our mediator were present” (Brenton, modernized).

verses.text:
I will say to God, ‘Do not condemn me;
make me know why you contend with me.

Is it good to you that you oppress,
that you despise the toil of your hands
and shine upon the counsel of the wicked?

Have you eyes of flesh,
or do you see as a man sees?

Are your days as the days of a mortal,
or your years as the days of a man,

that you seek after my iniquity
and search for my sin,

knowing as you do that I am not in the wrong,
and that from your hand no one can rescue?

“ ‘Your hands shaped me and made me,
all of me round about; yet you would swallow me up?

Remember, I pray, that you made me like clay;
and to the dust will you return me?

Did you not pour me out like milk
and curdle me like cheese?

With skin and flesh you clothed me,
and with bones and sinews you knit me together.

Life and steadfast love you have granted me,
and your care has watched over my spirit.

Yet these things you kept concealed in your heart;
I am aware that this was your intent:

if I sinned, you would watch me
and would not acquit me of my iniquity.

If I am wicked, woe to me!
And if I am righteous, I cannot lift up my head,
being sated with shame and looking upon my affliction.

And should it lift itself up, like a lion you would hunt me,
and again you would show yourself wonderful against me.

“ ‘Why then did you bring me out from the womb?
I would have breathed my last, and no eye would have seen me.

I would have been as though I had not been,
carried from the belly to the grave.

Are not my days few? Then cease,{b}
and let me alone, that I may brighten a little,

before I go, and return not,
to the land of darkness and deep shadow,

notes.text: Or “relays of troops come against me”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
So the written Hebrew text; the scribal reading is “Cease, then, and set me alone.”
Hebrew ʿefatah, a rare word for deep darkness.

verses.text: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:

“Shall a multitude of words go unanswered,
and shall a man of lips{a} be counted in the right?

Shall your babble make men hold their peace,
and shall you mock with none to put you to shame?

For you say, ‘Spotless is my doctrine,
and in your sight I am pure.’

But O that God would speak,
and open his lips against you,

“The searching out of God—can you attain it?
The utmost bound of Shaddai—can you arrive at it?

Heights of the heavens—what can you do?
Deeper than Sheol—what can you know?

Longer than the earth is its measure,
and broader than the sea.

If he passes through and shuts up,
or calls an assembly, who can turn him back?

For he knows worthless men;
he sees iniquity, and will he not take note of it?

But an empty-headed man will gain understanding
when a wild donkey’s colt is born a man.{d}

“If you yourself set your heart aright
and spread out your palms toward him—

if iniquity is in your hand, put it far away,
and let not wrong dwell in your tents—

surely then you shall lift up your face without blemish;
you shall be firmly set, and shall not fear.

For you shall forget trouble;
like waters that have flowed past you shall remember it.

And brighter than noonday your life shall rise;
its darkness shall be like the morning.

And you shall trust, because there is hope;
you shall search about you{e} and lie down in safety.

You shall lie down, and none shall make you afraid;
and many shall court your favor.

notes.text: That is, a man full of talk.
Hebrew tushiyyah; see the note at 5:12.
Or “God causes some of your iniquity to be forgotten.”
Or “when a wild donkey is born tame”; the proverb is uncertain.
Or “you shall dig” (that is, set up your tent); the Hebrew is uncertain.

verses.text: Then Job answered and said:

“Doubtless you are the people,
and with you wisdom will die!

For misfortune there is contempt, in the thought of one at ease;
it is ready for those whose feet slip.{a}

“But ask now the beasts, and they will teach you,
and the birds of the heavens, and they will tell you;

or speak to the earth,{c} and it will teach you;
and the fish of the sea will recount it to you.

Which of all these knows not
that it is Yahweh’s{d} hand that has wrought this?

In his hand is the soul of every living thing,
and the breath of all flesh of man.

Is it not the ear that tries out words,
even as the mouth tastes its meat?

With the aged is wisdom,
and length of days is understanding.

“With him are wisdom and might;
his are counsel and understanding.

See, he tears down, and it shall not be built;
he shuts in a man, and there shall be no opening.

See, he holds back the waters, and they dry up;
he sends them out, and they overturn the land.

With him are strength and sound wisdom;{e}
the one led astray and the one who leads astray are his.

He leads counselors away stripped,
and of judges he makes fools.

The bond of kings he loosens,
and binds a waistcloth on their loins.

He leads priests away stripped,
and overthrows the long-established.

He takes away the speech of the trusted,
and the discernment of the elders he removes.

He pours contempt upon nobles,
and the girdle of the mighty he slackens.

He uncovers deep things out of darkness
and brings deep shadow out to the light.

He makes nations great, and destroys them;
he spreads nations abroad, and leads them away.

He takes away the heart of the chiefs of the people of the land,
and makes them wander in a trackless waste.

They grope in the dark without light,
and he makes them stagger like a drunken man.

notes.text: The Hebrew of this verse is uncertain.
Or “whom God has brought into his hand”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Or “the plants of the earth.”
This is the only place in the poetic dialogue (3:1–42:6) where the name Yahweh appears outside the headings of the divine speeches; some Hebrew manuscripts read “God” (Eloah). Compare Isaiah 41:20.
Hebrew tushiyyah; see the note at 5:12.

verses.text:
“See, all this my eye has seen;
my ear has heard and understood it.

What you know, I also know;
I fall not beneath you.

But I would speak to Shaddai,
and to argue my case with God I desire.

But you are plasterers of lies;
physicians of no worth are you all.

O that you would keep utterly silent,
and it would be accounted wisdom to you!

Hear now my argument,
and to the pleas of my lips give heed.

Will you speak wrong on God’s behalf,
and for him speak deceit?

Will you show him partiality?
Will you plead the case for God?

Will it be good when he searches you out?
Or as one mocks a man, will you mock him?

Reprove you he surely shall,
if you favor faces in secret.

Will not his loftiness strike terror into you,
and the fear of him fall heavy on you?

Your memorable sayings are proverbs of ashes;
your defenses are defenses of clay.

“Be silent before me, and I will speak;
then let come upon me what may.

Why should I take my flesh in my teeth
and put my life in my palm?{a}

See, he will slay me; I have no hope;{b}
yet my ways I will argue to his face.

This too shall be my salvation,
that no godless man shall come before him.

Listen closely to my words,
and let my declaration be in your ears.

See now, I have set my case in order;
I know that I shall be found in the right.

Who is he that will contend with me?
For then I would be silent and breathe my last.

“Only two things do not do to me;
then from your face I will not hide myself:

Remove your palm far off from me,
and let no dread of you affright me.

Then call, and I will answer;
or let me speak, and do you reply to me.

How many are my iniquities and sins?
Make me know my transgression and my sin.

For what cause do you hide your face
and reckon me your foe?{c}

Will you harass a leaf blown about,
and chase after withered chaff?

For you write bitter things against me,
and make me inherit the iniquities of my youth.

And he{e} wastes away like a rotten thing,
like a garment that the moth has eaten.

notes.text: That is, why should I risk my life?
So the written Hebrew text (loʾ, “not”). The scribal reading (lo, “in him”) gives the familiar sense, “Though he slay me, yet I will hope in him.” The line is a well-known crux.
Hebrew ʾoyev, a play on Job’s name, ʾIyyov.
Or “you draw a line”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
That is, man; this verse may belong after 14:2.

verses.text:
“Man, born of woman,
is short of days and sated with trouble.

Like a flower he comes forth and withers;
he flees like the shadow and does not stay.

And upon such a one do you open your eyes,
and bring me{a} into judgment with you?

Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?
Not one!

If his days are determined,
the number of his months is with you,
and you have appointed his limits that he cannot pass,

look away from him, that he may cease,
until he finds pleasure, like a hireling, in his day.

Though its root grow old in the earth,
and its stump die in the dust,

at the scent of water it will bud
and put forth a branch like a young plant.

But a man dies and is laid low;
a man breathes his last, and where is he?

Waters fail from a lake,
and a river dries up and is parched;

“O that you would hide me in Sheol,
conceal me until your anger turns back,
appoint me a set time and remember me!

If a man dies, shall he live again?
All the days of my hard service I would wait,
until my relief{b} should come.

You would call, and I would answer you;
for the work of your hands you would long.

For then my steps you would count,
yet not lie in wait over my sin.

Sealed up in a bag would be my transgression,
and you would plaster over my iniquity.

“Yet a mountain falling wears away to nothing,
and a crag is shifted out of its place;

You overpower him forever, and he passes on;
you change his face and send him away.

His sons come to honor, and he knows it not;
they are brought low, but he perceives it not of them.

Only his own flesh upon him feels pain,
and his own soul within him mourns.”

notes.text: The Septuagint (Brenton: “caused him to enter into judgment”), Syriac, and Vulgate read “him.”
Hebrew ḥalifah, “change,” “renewal,” or “relief” (as of a guard).

verses.text: Then Eliphaz the Temanite answered and said:

“Should a wise man answer with windy knowledge,
and fill his belly with the east wind?

Should he argue with talk that profits not,
or with words by which he does no good?

But you, you are making void the fear of God,
and curtailing devotion before God.

For your iniquity instructs your mouth,
and you choose the tongue of the crafty.

Your own mouth condemns you, and not I;
your own lips testify against you.

“Were you the first man to be born?
Or before the hills were you brought forth?

Did you hearken in God’s secret council?
Have you drawn off wisdom for yourself alone?

What do you know that we know not?
What do you understand that is not with us?

Gray heads and old men alike are with us,
men greater in days than your own father.

Are the consolations of God too small for you,
and a word dealt gently with you?

Why does your heart sweep you off,
and wherefore do your eyes wink,{a}

that you turn your spirit against God
and let words go forth from your mouth?

What is man, that he should be clean,
or one born of woman, that he should be righteous?

See, in his holy ones he puts no trust,
and the heavens are not clean in his eyes;

how much less one who is abominable and corrupt,
a man who drinks injustice like water!

“I will declare it to you; hearken to me;
what I have beheld I will relate,

what wise men have told,
and their fathers did not conceal,

to whom alone the land was given,
and no stranger passed among them:

All the days of the wicked man he writhes in pain,
and the number of years laid up for the ruthless.

A sound of terrors is in his ears;
in peace the destroyer comes upon him.

He does not believe that he will return out of darkness,
and he is marked out for the sword.

He wanders abroad for bread—‘Where is it?’{b}
He knows that a day of darkness is ready at his hand.

Straits and distress put him in dread;
they overpower him, as a king equipped for the charge.{c}

Because he stretched out his hand against God
and played the mighty man against Shaddai,

running against him with outstretched neck,{d}
with the thick bosses of his shields;

because he covered his face with his fat
and gathered fat upon his loins,

he shall not be rich, nor shall his wealth endure,
nor shall their possessions{e} bend to the earth.

Let him not trust in emptiness, deceiving himself,
for emptiness shall be his recompense.

Before his day it shall be fulfilled,
and his palm branch shall not be green.

Like a vine he shall drop his unripe grapes,
and like an olive cast off his flowers.

For barren is the band of the profane,
and fire eats the tents where bribes are taken.

They conceive mischief and bring forth iniquity,
and their belly prepares deceit.”

notes.text: Hebrew razam, found only here; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps “wink” or “flash.”
Or, by a slight change following the Septuagint, “He is appointed as food for the vulture”; Brenton: “he has been appointed to be food for vultures.”
Hebrew kidor, found only here; the meaning “onset” or “attack” is uncertain.
Or “with stiff neck.”
Hebrew minlam, found only here; the meaning is uncertain.
That is, God’s.

verses.text: Then Job answered and said:

“Many such things have I heard;
troublesome comforters are you all.

Is there an end to windy words?
Or what provokes you, that you answer?

I too could speak as you do,
if your soul were in my soul’s place;
I could join words together against you
and shake my head at you.

I could strengthen you with my mouth,
and the solace of my lips would hold back your pain.

“If I speak, my pain is not held back;
and if I forbear, what departs from me?

But now he has wearied me;
you have made desolate all my company.

And you have shriveled me up;{a} it is become a witness;
and my leanness rises up against me; it testifies to my face.

God delivers me up to the unjust
and casts me into the hands of the wicked.

He breaches me, breach after breach;
like a warrior he rushes at me.

Sackcloth have I sewn upon my skin,
and have thrust my horn{c} into the dust.

My face is red with weeping,
and on my eyelids is deep shadow,

although there is no violence in my hands,
and my prayer is pure.

“O earth, cover not my blood,
and let there be no resting place for my cry.

Even now, see, my witness is in the heavens,
and he who vouches for me is on high.{d}

My interpreters{e} are my friends;
to God my eye drips tears,

that he would argue the case of a man with God,
as a son of man does for his neighbor.

For a few years more shall come,
and on a path of no return I shall go.

notes.text: Hebrew qamat, a rare word; perhaps “seized” or “shriveled.”
Or “his arrows”; Hebrew rabbav, a rare word.
That is, my strength or dignity.
Hebrew sahed, an Aramaic word for “witness” found only here in the Hebrew Bible. Who this witness is—God himself, or a heavenly advocate—is debated; compare 9:33 and 19:25.
Or “My scorners”; Hebrew melitsay can mean either.

verses.text:
“My breath is spent; my days are snuffed out;
for me the burial places wait.

Surely mockers are with me,
and on their provocation my eye must dwell.

Lay down, I pray, a pledge for me with yourself;
who else is there that will strike hands with me?{a}

For you have hidden their heart from understanding;
therefore you will not exalt them.

He who denounces friends for a share of spoil—
the eyes of his children shall fail.

But he has made me a byword of the peoples,
and one in whose face men spit.

Dim has my eye grown for grief,
and my limbs are all as a shade.

Upright men are aghast at this,
and the guiltless rouses himself against the profane.

But the just man keeps hold of his path,
and the clean of hands adds strength to strength.

But as for you all, come back now, I pray;
I shall not find a wise man among you.

“Gone by are my days; snapped are my purposes,
the cherished wishes{b} of my heart.

Night they turn into day;
‘Light is close at hand,’ they say, before the face of darkness.

If I hope for Sheol as my house,
if in the darkness I spread out my couch,

if I say to the pit,{c} ‘You are my father,’
to the worm, ‘My mother and my sister,’

where then is my hope?
And my hope—who shall see it?

Shall it go down to the gates of Sheol?
Shall we sink down together into the dust?”

notes.text: That is, who will stand surety for me?
Hebrew morashe, “possessions”; here perhaps “cherished desires.”

Or “to corruption”; Hebrew shaḥat. With this verse begin the surviving fragments of the Aramaic Targum of Job from Qumran Cave 11 (11QtgJob), which is reported to preserve portions of 17:14–42:11 and to end at 42:11.

verses.text: Then Bildad the Shuhite answered and said:

“How long will you set snares{a} for words?
Consider, and afterward we will speak.

Why are we reckoned as cattle,
counted unclean{b} in your eyes?

“Indeed, the lamp of the wicked shall be quenched,
and no spark of his fire shall glow.

The light grows dark in his tent,
and his lamp above him is put out.

His mighty strides are cramped,
and his own counsel casts him down.

For he is thrust into a net by his own feet,
and upon a mesh he walks.

A gin grips him by the heel;
a trap holds him fast.

A noose for him is hidden in the ground,
and a trap for him upon the path.

Terrors on every side affright him
and chase him at his heels.

His strength is famished,
and calamity is ready at his side.

It eats away the members of his skin;
death’s firstborn{c} eats up his limbs.

He is plucked out of his tent, his safe place,
and they make him march to the king of terrors.

In his tent dwells that which is none of his;{d}
brimstone is scattered over his habitation.

Beneath, his roots dry up,
and above, his branch withers.

The memory of him is lost from the land,
and no name is his in the open places.

They thrust him from light into darkness
and chase him out of the world.

He has neither offspring nor descendant among his people,
nor any survivor where he sojourned.

At his day those of the west are appalled,
and those of the east are seized with horror.{e}

Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous,
and this is the place of him who knows not God.”

notes.text: Hebrew qintse, found only here; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps “ends” or “snares.”
Or “stupid”; Hebrew nitminu, of uncertain meaning.
Probably a deadly disease, personified as death’s eldest son.
Or “Nothing of his dwells in his tent”; the Hebrew is uncertain.
Or “Those who come after are appalled at his day, and those who went before are seized with horror.”

verses.text: Then Job answered and said:

“How long will you torment my soul
and crush me with words?

Ten times over now you have insulted me;
without shame you deal hardly with me.{a}

And even if in truth I have erred,
my error lodges with me.

If indeed you will magnify yourselves against me
and argue my disgrace against me,

then know that it is God who has dealt crookedly with me
and has thrown his net round about me.

“See, I cry out, ‘Violence!’ but I am not answered;
I shout for help, but there is no justice.

My way he has walled up, and I cannot pass,
and upon my paths he sets darkness.

My glory he has stripped from me
and taken the crown from my head.

He breaks me down on every side, and I am gone,
and my hope he has pulled up like a tree.

He has kindled his anger against me
and counts me as one of his adversaries.

“My brothers he has put far from me,
and those who know me are wholly estranged from me.

My kinsmen have failed,
and my intimate friends have forgotten me.

The guests in my house and my maidservants count me a stranger;
a foreigner I have become in their eyes.

I call to my servant, and he gives no answer;
with my own mouth I must entreat him.

My breath is strange to my wife,
and I am loathsome to the sons of my own womb.{b}

Even young children despise me;
when I rise, they speak against me.

All the men of my counsel abhor me,
and those whom I loved have turned against me.

To my skin and to my flesh my bone cleaves,
and I have escaped by the skin of my teeth.{c}

Have pity on me, have pity on me, O you my friends,
for the hand of God has touched me!

Why do you pursue me as God does,
and are not satisfied with my flesh?{d}

“O that my words were now written!
O that they were inscribed in a book,

with a pen of iron and lead
forever cut into the rock!

But I—I know that my redeemer{e} lives,
and at the last{f} he will stand up upon the dust.{g}

And after my skin has been thus stripped off,
yet from my flesh{h} I shall see God,

If you should say, ‘How shall we hound him?’
and, ‘The root of the trouble lies in him,’{k}

notes.text: Hebrew tahkeru, found only here; the meaning is uncertain, perhaps “wrong” or “stun.”
That is, my own brothers, born of the same womb as I. The Septuagint reads “I entreated the sons of my concubines” (Brenton, modernized).
The meaning of this proverbial phrase is uncertain; it may mean “with nothing at all left.”
That is, by slandering me (compare the Aramaic idiom “eat pieces of” for accusing).

Hebrew goʾel, the next of kin who buys back a relative’s property, frees him from slavery, or avenges his blood (Leviticus 25:25; Numbers 35:19; Ruth 4:1–6); hence “vindicator” or “champion.” Whether Job means God himself or another heavenly figure (compare 9:33; 16:19) is debated. Verses 25–27 are among the most difficult in the book; nearly every line is uncertain.
Or “as the last”; Hebrew ʾaḥaron.

Or “upon the earth,” or “over my dust” (that is, my grave). The Septuagint reads verses 25–26a: “For I know that he is eternal who is about to deliver me, and to raise up upon the earth my skin that endures these sufferings” (Brenton, modernized).
Or “apart from my flesh” (that is, after death) or “in my flesh”; the Hebrew preposition min can mean either “from (within)” or “without.”
Or “and not as a stranger.”
The kidneys were thought of as the seat of the emotions; that is, my heart faints with longing.
So many Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint, and the Vulgate; most Hebrew manuscripts read “in me.”
Hebrew shaddun, of uncertain meaning; some read “that there is a Judge” or “that there is Shaddai.”

verses.text: Then Zophar the Naamathite answered and said:

“Therefore my disquieting thoughts make me answer,
because of the haste that is within me.

Reproof that insults me I hear,
and out of my understanding a spirit answers me.

Is this not known to you from ancient days,
from the time man was set on the earth,

that the triumphing of the wicked is short,
and the joy of the godless but for a moment?

Though his height mount up to the heavens,
and his head reach to the clouds,

like his own dung he shall perish forever;
those who saw him shall say, ‘Where is he?’

Like a dream he flies away, and they find him not;
he is chased away like a vision of the night.

The eye that glimpsed him does so no more,
nor does his place behold him any longer.

His sons shall seek the favor of the poor,{a}
and his own hands shall give back his wealth.

His bones were full of his youthful vigor,
but with him it shall lie down in the dust.

“Though evil be sweet in his mouth,
though he hide it under his tongue,

though he spare it and will not let it go,
but hold it back within his palate,

his food is turned in his bowels;
it is the venom of cobras within him.

Wealth he has gulped down, and he shall spew it up;
out of his belly God shall drive it.

He sucks the poison of cobras;
the tongue of the viper{b} slays him.

He shall not gaze upon the brooks,
the torrents running with honey and curds.

He gives back the gain of his toil and does not swallow it;
from the profit of his trading he gets no enjoyment.

For the poor he has oppressed and abandoned;
a house he seized, though he did not build it.

“Because he knew no quiet in his belly,
he shall not escape with what he desires.

There was nothing left that he did not devour;
therefore his prosperity shall not endure.

In the fullness of his plenty he shall be in straits;
every hand of the wretched shall come upon him.

He shall flee from the iron weapon;
a bow of bronze shall pierce him through.

The heavens shall reveal his iniquity,
and the earth shall rise up against him.

The increase of his house shall depart,
flowing away in the day of his{e} anger.

This is the portion of a wicked man from God,
and the heritage appointed to him by God.”

notes.text: Or “The poor shall oppress his sons.”
Hebrew ʾefʿeh, a poisonous snake; the exact species is uncertain.
Hebrew “he.”
Hebrew biletumo, of uncertain meaning; perhaps “into his flesh” or “as his food.”
That is, God’s.

verses.text: Then Job answered and said:

“Hear, O hear my word,
and let this be your consolation.

Bear with me, and I will speak;
and after I have spoken, mock on.

As for me, is my complaint against man?
And why should I not be impatient?

Turn to me and be appalled,
and lay your hand upon your mouth.

When I call it to mind, I am thrown into dismay,
and a shuddering takes hold of my flesh.

“Why do the wicked live on,
grow old, yes, grow mighty in power?

Their offspring are established in their sight with them,
and their descendants before their eyes.

Their houses are at peace, without fear,
and no rod of God is upon them.

Their bull breeds and does not fail;
their cow calves and does not miscarry.

They send out their little ones like a flock,
and their children dance about.

They lift up their voices to timbrel and lyre
and rejoice at the sound of the pipe.

They spend their days in prosperity,
and in a moment they go down to Sheol.{a}

Yet they say to God, ‘Depart from us!
We have no desire for the knowledge of your ways.

What is Shaddai, that we should serve him?
And what does it profit us if we entreat him?’

See, is not their prosperity in their own hand?
The counsel of the wicked is far from me.

“How often is the lamp of the wicked put out,
and does their calamity come upon them?
How often does he apportion pains in his anger?

How often are they as stubble in the face of the wind,
as chaff whirled off by the tempest?

You say, ‘God stores up his iniquity for his sons.’
Let him repay it to the man himself, that he may know it!

Let his own eyes see his destruction,
and let him drink of the wrath of Shaddai.

For what does he care for his house after him,
when the number of his months is cut off?

Shall anyone teach God knowledge,
seeing that he judges those on high?

One dies in his full strength,
wholly at ease and secure,

his pails{b} full of milk
and the marrow of his bones moist.

And another dies with a bitter soul,
having never eaten of good things.

Alike they lie down in the dust,
and the worm covers them.

“See, I know your thoughts,
and the schemes by which you would wrong me.

For you say, ‘Where is the house of the prince?
And where is the tent in which the wicked dwelt?’

Have you never inquired of the wayfarers?
Do you not acknowledge their signs,

that on the day of calamity the evil man is spared,
on the day of wrath they are led away?{c}

Who declares his way to his face?
And for what he has done, who repays him?

When he is carried to the graves,
watch is kept over his tomb.

How then do you comfort me with emptiness,
when of your answers there remains only faithlessness?”

notes.text: Or “in peace they go down to Sheol.”
Hebrew ʿatinav, found only here; the meaning is uncertain: perhaps “his pails” or “his haunches.” The Septuagint reads “his inwards are full of fat” (Brenton, modernized).
That is, they are rescued; or “from the day of wrath they are led away.”
